newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Taiwan use of LNG in power seen surging - report.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan use of LNG in power seen surging - report.

text.p: Taiwan's natural gas-fired power will account for 20.2 percent of the island's total power capacity in 2010, up from only 5.1 percent in 1995, the state Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) said.
By the end of 1995, Taiwanese power plants had installed capacity 23,964 million watts, of which 5.1 percent was gas-fired, CPC said in a report, submitted in paper for a gas conference in Singapore.
Fuel oil, coal and nuclear power accounted for 22.7 percent, 24.6 percent and 21.5 percent respectively of the total, it said.
However, by the year 2010, gas-fired capacity would show the biggest jump in use, rising to 20.2 percent of the total 56,600 million watts.
Fuel oil, coal and nuclear would account for 15.0 percent, 22.5 percent and 21.8 percent respectively in 2010, the report said.

Taiwan, with hardly any of its own energy sources, has imported an annual 1.5 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Indonesia since 1990. The imports are expected to reach 3.34 million tonnes in 1998, the report said.
The island has also imported natural gas from Malaysia since 1995 and the imports will gradually increase to 2.25 million tonnes, it said.
Taiwan's natural gas demand totalled 2.28 million tonnes in 1995, compared with domestic production of 590,000 tonnes.
In 2010, demand is expected to soar to 8.45 million tonnes in 2010, compared with domestic output of 523,000 tonnes.
By then, Taiwan is expected to import 7.94 million tonnes of natural gas, the report said.
